A bit later — plans and soft-nos

the wait-a-moment promise — also its doubled form (in the example below) = right away. Standard layer: yíhuì (the written form).

sentence-final tag

"..., you know / that's how it is" — tags a whole statement as obviously true; softens urges (zǒu sá!). Locals write it 撒.
Tāmen de yìsi hěn míngxiǎn sá!

Dear or beloved (way of starting a letter)

Glue — grammar

descriptive complement V + de + Adj

Template: V + de + Adj/phrase

how an action is done — compliments and critiques ride on it

Tā pǎo de hěn kuài.
Nǐ xiě de zì zhēn piàoliang.

Foreigner traps

  • The adjective goes AFTER the verb: shuō de hǎo, never hǎo shuō de — English order is the trap.
  • Careful writing spells this de 得 — same sound as possessive de, different character, zero difference in speech.
  • Asking 'how well?' swaps the slot: Tā shuō de zěnmeyàng? — the question word takes the adjective's seat.

potential complements (can/can't manage it)

Template: V + de bu + liǎo / dòng / qǐ (chī bu liǎo "can't finish eating," ná bu dòng "can't lift it")

ability focused on the outcome, not the bare act

Zhème dà de xínglixiāng, wǒ ná bu dòng.
Míngtiān wǒ lái bu jí, hòutiān ba.

Foreigner traps

  • bu is fused and toneless: ná bu dòng never surfaces a full 4th-tone bù — the clipped 'bu' IS the grammar.
  • The pair flips on the middle syllable: chī de liǎo (can finish it) vs chī bu liǎo (can't) — potential goes both ways.
  • néng chī states ability in the abstract; chī bu xià says the meal is happening to you now — refusals want the second.

Native notes — the polite no, deflected praise, and Chongqing's wait-a-bit

Potential complements are the polite no

qù bu liǎo, chī bu xià, lái bu jí turn refusals into physics: you'd love to, but the universe won't allow it. That's why natives reach for them over bù néng when declining invitations — blame-free, face-saving, and they still hold as a no. Accept the convention and decline like a local.

nǎlǐ nǎlǐ deflects praise

A compliment is bounced, not caught: Nǐ tài bàng le draws Nǎlǐ nǎlǐ (literally 'where, where' — not at all) or the slightly modern guòjiǎng. Accepting with a plain xièxie is grammatically fine but reads less modest; the double nǎlǐ is the culturally fluent serve.

The dismissal ladder

suàn le (drop it) → dé le (oh, stop) → gòu le (enough!) climbs in irritation; xíng ba is the reluctant yes on the same ladder family. Natives position themselves on it constantly — hear the temperature, not the dictionary gloss, and match the rung when you answer.

Chongqing wait-a-bit and the sá tag

Today's two dialect cards pair up in daily life: the wait-a-bit promise (buy minutes, promise seconds with the doubled form — standard layer: yíhuì / mǎshàng) and sá, the sentence-final tag that marks a statement as obviously true: zǒu sá! Soft, local, everywhere — and verified in the field guide.
